Four monosyllable workhorses

day; sky

Wǒ jīntiān máng le yì tiān

matter, thing, business

casual speech usually adds erhua: shìr ("a thing/matter").
Yǒu shìr ma?

to do (blunt)

blunt "do"; in questions it usually shows up as gànmá ("what for/doing what").
Nǐ zài gànmá?

to die; (intensifier)

as V + sǐ le it means "…to death," not literal dying (lèi sǐ le = dead tired).
Lèi sǐ wǒ le!

Glue — grammar

gěi, the benefactive hub

Template: gěi + person + V ("for/to someone"); V + gěi + person ("V it to them")

all favors, gifts, calls, and payments route through gěi

Native notes — filler, refusals, and friendship maintenance

nèige is the 'um' of spoken Mandarin

Said slowly with a rising-falling drift, nèige (that-one) is the universal hesitation filler — you will hear it mid-sentence everywhere once you know it. Hearing it as filler rather than 'that' is a listening milestone; using it naturally in hesitation rhythm is one of the strongest accidental fluency signals.

Refusals trail off, they don't land

Direct bù xíng is rare between friends. The native refusal is a trailing kěshì... a (but... though), or a deferral: dào shíhou zài shuō (we'll see). Yǒu shìr ma? asked flatly can itself be a soft pushback ('what do you want?'). When you hear 'we'll see' after a concrete proposal, read it as a probable no and don't push.

xīnlèi is heart-tired, not body-tired

lèi sǐ le is physical exhaustion (or its exaggeration); xīnlèi is emotional — draining people, one-sided effort. They call for different sympathy: offer rest for lèi, offer listening for xīnlèi. The texting-burnout pair yǐdú bùhuí (left on read) and wúyǔ live in the xīnlèi world.

Reply speed is caring

In Chinese friendship maintenance, fast replies signal valuing the person; slow replies need an excuse (máng sǐ le — dead busy). This is why yǐdú bùhuí stings enough to have its own slang — being seen-and-ignored is a small statement. Apologize for slow replies with a Gàng kàn dào (just saw it), the universal amnesty.
